nameStory: The 'bristly' in bristly crowfoot comes from the rough, hairy texture of its stems and leaves that you can actually feel when you brush against them. The name 'crowfoot' refers to the deeply divided leaf shape that resembles a bird's foot with spreading toes. Some also call it Pennsylvania buttercup, named after the state where it was first scientifically described.
description: Bristly crowfoot is a somewhat scrappy-looking member of the buttercup family that stands out more for its texture than its beauty. This annual plant grows 1-3 feet tall with a branching, upright habit and notably hairy stems and leaves that feel rough to the touch. Unlike its showier buttercup cousins, it produces small, pale yellow flowers that are easy to overlook. The deeply divided leaves give it a delicate, feathery appearance that contrasts with its coarse, bristly feel.

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Stems and leaves are noticeably hairy and rough to the touch - run your finger along a stem and you'll feel the bristly texture that gives this plant its name

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small, pale yellow flowers about 1/4 inch across with 5 petals that are much less showy than other buttercups - often described as looking rather sickly or washed-out

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Deeply divided into narrow segments that spread out like fingers, giving a lacy or feathery appearance, and covered in short, stiff hairs

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Upright annual that branches extensively, creating a somewhat messy, sprawling appearance unlike the neater growth of perennial buttercups

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Forms clusters of small, flattened seeds with tiny hooked beaks that can catch on clothing or animal fur

habitat: Look for bristly crowfoot in wet, disturbed areas like muddy shores of ponds and streams, ditches, wet meadows, and marshy spots. It thrives in places that get seasonally flooded or stay consistently moist, often growing alongside sedges, rushes, and other water-loving plants. This plant seems to prefer areas with some soil disturbance rather than pristine wetlands.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge as small rosettes with the characteristic deeply divided, bristly leaves becoming noticeable as temperatures warm.
seasonality.summer: Blooms from mid to late summer with small pale yellow flowers, and the bristly texture of stems and leaves is most pronounced during active growth.
seasonality.fall: Seeds mature and disperse in early fall, while the entire plant begins to yellow and die back as it completes its annual cycle.
seasonality.winter: No above-ground parts remain visible as this is an annual plant, but seeds lie dormant in muddy soil waiting for spring.

funFact: Despite being in the buttercup family known for bright, cheerful yellow flowers, bristly crowfoot's blooms are so pale and small that they almost look like they're trying to hide - it's like the plant put all its energy into growing defensive bristles and forgot to make attractive flowers!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other small-flowered buttercups, but the bristly, rough texture is your best clue - other buttercups in wet areas tend to have smoother, less hairy leaves and stems. Memory trick: if it feels like you're petting a cactus when you touch the leaves, it's probably bristly crowfoot.
contextualKnowledge: The term 'crowfoot' versus 'buttercup' for the same plant family can be confusing - generally 'crowfoot' is used for the less showy, often wetland species, while 'buttercup' refers to the bright yellow, more garden-like species. Both names refer to plants in the genus Ranunculus.
compareHints: Among New England buttercups, bristly crowfoot stands out for its rough, hairy texture and pale flowers - most other buttercups have smoother leaves and bright golden-yellow blooms. The similar cursed crowfoot also has small pale flowers but lacks the bristly texture and has more succulent-looking leaves. Bristly crowfoot's annual growth habit also distinguishes it from most perennial buttercups that form spreading colonies.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's buttercups, small-flowered buttercup is unmistakable due to its tiny petals - all other buttercup species have much more prominent yellow flowers.
Among New England's buttercups, hooked buttercup is unique for its woodland habitat and tiny, pale flowers—most other buttercups prefer sunny, open areas and have much brighter, larger yellow blooms.
Among New England's many buttercup species, meadow buttercup stands out for its tall, upright growth and deeply palm-divided leaves.
Unlike meadow buttercup which grows in upright clumps, or bulbous buttercup with its swollen stem base, creeping buttercup is the only common buttercup that spreads by runners along the ground.
Among New England's many buttercup species, bulbous buttercup is the only one with that distinctive swollen stem base.
Unlike other New England buttercups that have bright, showy yellow flowers, cursed crowfoot has tiny, pale, almost insignificant blooms.
Among New England's many buttercups, yellow water-crowfoot is one of the few truly aquatic species, distinguished by its floating stems and dramatic leaf differences between air and water.
Among New England's buttercups, creeping spearwort is unique for its simple, narrow leaves - all other local buttercups have divided or lobed leaves.
Unlike the robust meadow buttercup or creeping buttercup with their typical three-lobed leaves, fen crowfoot has leaves so finely divided they look almost thread-like.

Among New England's many buttercups, early buttercup stands out for its combination of very early bloom time, preference for dry rather than moist habitats, and distinctively narrow, deeply-cut leaves.
Unlike the common meadow buttercup which grows tall and robust in fields, Allegheny Mountain buttercup stays much smaller and more delicate.
Rock buttercup stands out from other New England buttercups by having the smallest, palest flowers in the family - most other buttercups have bright golden-yellow blooms.
Among the 20+ buttercup species in New England, lesser spearwort stands out immediately because of its narrow, spear-shaped leaves – all other buttercups have lobed, divided, or rounded leaves.
Unlike the common meadow buttercup which prefers drier ground and grows much taller, swamp buttercup stays low and spreads along wet soil.
Among New England's aquatic buttercups, longbeak buttercup is distinguished by its exceptionally long fruit beaks and preference for flowing water.

Among New England's many buttercups, bristly buttercup stands out primarily for its rough, hairy texture - most other species like meadow buttercup and creeping buttercup have relatively smooth stems and leaves.

Unlike terrestrial buttercups like meadow buttercup or creeping buttercup, small yellow water-crowfoot is adapted for aquatic life with thicker, more succulent leaves and a strictly prostrate growth habit.
Unlike all other New England buttercups that grow upright, Lapland buttercup stays completely flat and creeping.
Among New England's many buttercups, water-plantain spearwort is unique for its completely undivided, lance-shaped leaves - most other buttercups have deeply lobed or divided leaves.
Unlike its terrestrial buttercup cousins that have typical yellow flowers, thread-leaved water-crowfoot has white petals with yellow centers and specialized underwater foliage.
